list.listitem: Although a variety of mechanisms have been proposed for the development of avascular necrosis of the femoral head, no single etiology has been identified; however, the basic mechanism involves impaired circulation to a specific area that ultimately results in osteonecrosis. Consider avascular necrosis in patients with bone pain and risk factors, especially trauma, prolonged glucocorticoid use, or alcoholism. C
Order anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiographs as the initial imaging; order MRI if initial radiographs are nondiagnostic despite a high index of suspicion. B

The mainstay of treatment for avascular necrosis is surgical; the goal of therapy is to preserve the native joint for as long as possible. C However, authors of a network meta-analysis found no statistical difference in the outcomes of radiographic progression or conversion to total hip arthroplasty for femoral head osteonecrosis between core decompression techniques compared to non-operative therapy with the exception of less radiographic progression with core decompression plus cell therapy vs. nonsurgical treatment. B
Core decompression may be most beneficial in stages 0, 1, or 2. Osteotomy may be superior for later stage 2 or 3, and arthroplasty is indicated in stage 4 disease. B
Alendronate (70 mg/wk for 25 weeks) may prevent collapse of the femoral head and decrease hip replacement in patients with early nontraumatic osteonecrosis, but studies are conflicting. B

background.definition: Avascular necrosis (also called osteonecrosis, aseptic necrosis, and ischemic necrosis) is a disease resulting from the temporary or permanent loss of blood supply to the bones.

list.listitem: 10,000 to 20,000 new patients per year in the United States.

Sixty-seven to 69 cases/100,000 patient-years of medication use for bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw among Swedish patients aged 45 years or older. The incidence of background jaw osteonecrosis was 0.09 to 0.14/100,000 person-years in the same age group.

Among patients with sequential use of anti-resorptive agents, authors of a systematic review found 12 studies and determined a weighted, pooled prevalence rate of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw of 19% (95% CI 10%-27%) for sequential pamidronate-zoledronate therapy, 13% (95% CI 3%-22%) for sequential bisphosphonate-denosumab therapy, and 10% (95% CI 3%-22%) for sequential ibandronate-zoledronate therapy compared to 5% (95% CI 0%-9%) for bisphosphonates only and 4% (95% CI 3%-5%) for denosumab only.

Internationally, the annual incidence of Legg-Calvé-Perthes' disease among children under age 15 years ranges from 0.2 per 100,000 to 19.1 per 100,000; whites appeared most affected and East Asians least affected.

A population-based registry in Sweden found an annual incidence of Perthes disease (Legg-Calve-Perthes disease) of 9.3 per 100,000 persons, with a 3:1 ration of boys to girls. A higher incidence was seen in lower income brackets.
Occurs with greater frequency in the third to fifth decades of life.
In a 5-year retrospective analysis, 16 of 122 patients (13.1%) aged 6 to 49 years homozygous for sickle cell disease developed avascular necrosis.
Avascular necrosis is the underlying diagnosis in approximately 10% of all total hip replacements.
Half of patients with nontraumatic avascular necrosis of femoral head have bilateral involvement.
Compromise of bone vasculature leading to death of bone and marrow cells.
A variety of traumatic and nontraumatic factors contribute to its etiology.
Traumatic etiologies are most often fractures or dislocations.
Nontraumatic etiologies are most often related to glucocorticoid use or excessive alcohol intake (these may cause more than 90% of avascular necrosis cases).
Medications such as bisphosphonates and denosumab have been linked to osteonecrosis of the jaw.
Idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis may be associated with certain osseous anatomical findings on preoperative CT scans.
Genetic factors also increase risk (see below).
Interruption of blood supply to bone with subsequent hyperemia, demineralization, trabecular thinning, and ultimately collapse.
May be the result of combined effects of metabolic factors, vascular damage, increased intraosseous pressure, and mechanical stress.

Emerging lines of evidence suggest the matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) are closely related to the susceptibility of osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH). Authors of a meta-analysis showed a strong association between MMP-8 rs11225394 gene and an increased risk of ONFH, and between MMP-8 rs2012390 gene and decreased risk of ONFH. In another study including patients with cancer and patients with osteoporosis, SNP rs2736308 on chromosome 8 was associated with an increased risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (odds ratio [OR] 2.74, 95% CI 2.09-3.39).

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Diabetes mellitus or impaired fasting blood sugar
Systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis

list.listitem: Patients requiring prolonged treatment with prednisone are at lower risk of avascular necrosis if doses are kept below 15 to 20 mg/d. B
Secondary prevention includes treatment of hyperlipidemia and diabetes, as well as minimizing alcohol intake. B

Earlier studies suggested that bisphosphonates may decrease the prevalence of collapse of the femoral head and decrease hip replacement in patients with early nontraumatic osteonecrosis; however, in a multicenter RCT there was no effect of alendronate compared with placebo for preventing radiographic progression and total hip arthroplasty at a mean follow-up of two years.
Screening newborns with clinical examination or ultrasound can identify those at increased risk for developmental hip dysplasia, but the net benefits of screening are not clear.
Of children detected by screening, 60% to 80% detected by physical examination and over 90% detected by ultrasound resolve without treatment.
Patients who require prolonged treatment with prednisone are at lower risk (less than 3%) if doses are kept below 15 to 20 mg/d.

Regular alcohol users have an increased risk that is dose dependent, with relative risks of 3.3, 9.8, and 17.9 for current consumers of less than 400, 400 to 1000, and more than 1000 mL/wk of alcohol, respectively, compared with controls.

Alendronate (70 mg/wk for 25 weeks) may slow progression to collapse of the femoral head in patients with early nontraumatic osteonecrosis. To prevent one patient with early osteonecrosis from undergoing joint replacement over 2 years of follow-up, one would need to treat two (95% CI 1-3) for 25 weeks.
Secondary prevention in patients with preexisting disease includes aggressive treatment of hyperlipidemia and diabetes, as well as minimization of alcohol intake.
Consider avascular necrosis in any individual with bone pain and risk factors, especially trauma, prolonged glucocorticoid use, or alcoholism. C
Order anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiographs for initial evaluation of suspected avascular necrosis of the femoral head. B
Order MRI if initial radiographs are negative or equivocal despite a high index of suspicion based on the history and physical. B
In patients for whom MRI cannot be performed, a bone scan with SPECT images is a reasonable alternative. C
Assessment of femoral head perfusion during modified Dunn for unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis has been shown to be an accurate predictor of subsequent osteonecrosis.

Differential.Differential_Features: Back pain, reflex changes, radiation below knee, MRI
Lack of risk factors, absence of bony sclerosis on radiographs
Disabling nontraumatic pain, osteopenia, pregnant woman or middle-aged man
Common cause of acute unilateral hip pain in children; resolves spontaneously in most cases

list.listitem: The diagnosis of avascular necrosis of the femoral head may be made by fulfilling any two of the following five criteria: (1) collapse of the femoral head or crescent sign, (2) demarcating sclerosis in the femoral head, (3) cold in hot on bone scan (doughnut sign), (4) band-like pattern on T1-weighted MRI image, and (5) trabecular and marrow necrosis on histology.
See for staging.

The most common presenting symptom of avascular necrosis is pain, usually described as a dull ache or throbbing. Weight-bearing and motion-induced pain are seen in most cases; rest pain occurs in two-thirds of patients and night pain in one-third. Symptoms may be bilateral but are usually unilateral.
The disease is most commonly seen in the femoral head followed by the humeral head, knees, small bones of the foot, ankle, and hand, vertebrae, and bony structures of the face.
The disease usually occurs in the hip but may also affect the humeral head, femoral condyles, proximal tibia, vertebrae, and small bones of hand and foot.
Groin pain is most common in patients with femoral head disease, followed by lateral thigh and buttock pain.

Limited range of motion may occur, and patients often report a progressive limp. Examination may show limitation of forced internal rotation and abduction of hip. Gait may be antalgic (short stance phase) or later a Trendelenburg gait may develop (lurching gait due to weakness of hip abductors and gluteal muscles).

Anteroposterior view of pelvis and anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiographs of hip may show patchy areas of sclerosis and lucency. With disease progression, a "crescent sign" appears as a well-defined sclerotic area just beneath the articular surface; this signifies subchondral fracture. The femoral head typically becomes more flattened with time, leading to degenerative changes within the acetabulum.

If initial radiographs are nondiagnostic despite symptoms, yet risk factors are suspicious for avascular necrosis, MRI is necessary to confirm the diagnosis; the earliest finding is a band-like pattern on T1-weighted images. MRI is more sensitive than plain radiographs or bone scans (91% in one study using older technology) and is 75% to 100% specific.

A bone scan with SPECT imaging is a reasonable alternative for the diagnosis of radiologically occult avascular necrosis; increased bone turnover at the junction of dead and reactive bone results in increased uptake surrounding a cold area ("doughnut sign"). SPECT is 85% sensitive and 100% specific.

Emago® software (Oral Diagnostic Systems, Amsterdam, Netherlands) used to perform digital subtraction on intraoral radiographs may be useful for detecting sclerotic changes observed in early stages of bisphosphonate-related jaw osteonecrosis.
The diagnostic approach to avascular necrosis is based on a high index of suspicion for patients with pain and presence of known or probable risk factors, especially high-dose steroid use.
Initial imaging is radiographs; if nondiagnostic but suspicion persists, order MRI.

A variety of nonoperative treatment regimens have been evaluated for treatment of pre-collapse disease, with varying success. Prospective, multicenter, randomized trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy of these regimens in altering the natural disease history. Conservative management is an option for asymptomatic cases of stage 0 or stage 1A disease. C
Consider core decompression for young/active patients with early stage 0, 1, or 2 disease to preserve the femoral head; osteotomy is superior to core decompression for later stage 2 or 3 disease. B
Total hip arthroplasty is the treatment of choice in stage 4 disease, or in older sedentary patients with lesser disease. B

In cases of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, however, authors of a network meta-analysis found no statistical difference in the outcomes of radiographic progression or conversion to total hip arthroplasty between core decompression techniques compared to non-operative therapy with the exception of less radiographic progression with core decompression plus cell therapy vs. nonsurgical treatment. B
Combination core decompression plus bone marrow-derived cell therapies appear to be more effective in reducing pain and rates of total hip arthroplasty than decompression alone. A
Conservative management of avascular necrosis is generally ineffective at halting the progression of disease.
Symptomatic treatment may include nonsteroidal agents or other analgesics.

Bisphosphonates may decrease pain and slow progression to femoral head collapse. In a two-year RCT of 52 patients with hip osteonecrosis (65 hips), alendronate was not successful in preventing the necessity for total hip arthroplasty, reducing disease progression, or improving life quality.
A prospective, randomized, open-label, multicenter trial also showed that zoledronate does not prevent femoral head collapse from osteonecrosis.

In a retrospective study of 36 patients with bilateral idiopathic osteonecrosis with at least one hip in the pre-collapsed stage, 6,000 units of enoxaparin daily for 12 weeks reduced progression to collapse compared with no enoxaparin (15/26 hips vs. 5/23 remained in the pre-collapse stage). Similar numbers of patients in both groups had a coagulation disorder (seven patients in the enoxaparin group and five patients in the comparison group).
The surgical management of hip avascular necrosis is controversial. Asymptomatic lesions with less than 15% involvement of the femoral head may resolve without surgical intervention.
Early stage 0 to 2 in young/active patients: core decompression may be best at preserving the femoral head.
Later stage 2 or 3: osteotomy may be the best option.
Stage 4, or older/sedentary patients: total hip replacement is the treatment of choice.

One trial with 46 participants found no difference in major complications after a mean follow up of 3 years between persons randomized to receive surgical core hip decompression plus physical therapy versus physical therapy alone.

In one small RCT, patients randomized to autologous bone marrow mononuclear cell instillation into the core tract after core decompression had improved clinical scores (Harris Hip score) and mean hip survival (MRI) compared to patients receiving core decompression only, especially among patents with adverse prognostic features at initial presentation.

In another RCT of 100 patients with early stage osteonecrosis, those randomized to autologous implantation of iliac crest bone marrow-derived mononuclear cells vs. core decompression had less progression at 60 months (2/53 vs. 10/44 [minus 6 drop-outs]). No complications in either group were reported.

Authors of a network meta-analysis of 17 RCTs including 784 patients (918 hips) with osteonecrosis of the femoral head, found no statistical difference in the outcomes of radiographic progression or conversion to total hip arthroplasty between core decompression techniques compared to non-operative therapy with the exception of less radiographic progression with core decompression plus cell therapy vs. nonsurgical treatment.

The latter finding was confirmed in two meta-analyses of surgical treatment for patients with osteonecrosis of the femoral head. The first included 265 core decompression procedures alone compared to 263 combined core decompression and bone marrow-derived cell therapies. At a mean follow up of 82 (24 to 360) months, patients in the combined treatment group had lower pain scores (mean difference: -12.88) and lower rates of total hip arthroplasty (47/226 vs. 93/226, OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.21-0.55). Failure rate and time to failure or total hip arthroplasty were not significantly different between groups. The second demonstrated similar findings of reduced pain and lower rate of total hip arthroplasty with combined therapy.

For patients with Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, authors of a systematic review found surgical (femoral varus osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy) vs. nonsurgical treatment for children over age 8 years at onset with lateral pillar B or B/C border class involvement was associated with improved Stulberg outcomes (a classification system of femoral head deformity). The reliability of the Stulberg classification, however, appears low.

Patients with sickle cell disease undergoing total hip arthroplasty compared to patients without sickle cell disease have poorer outcomes including longer hospital length of stay, increased rates of surgical complications, and higher rates of readmission and revision.
Microsurgical reconstruction and laser-assisted surgical treatment appear useful for patients with bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, based on case series reports.

In one retrospective study of 30 patients with osteoporotic vertebral fractures and noninfected avascular osteonecrosis who underwent vertebroplasty, compression and kyphosis continued to progress for 2 years or longer.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials suggested that using Chinese herbal medicine formulas as adjunctive therapy may improve the effectiveness of core decompression for patients with avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with 630 patients with early and middle-stage osteonecrosis of the femoral head found acupuncture and moxibustion adjunctive treatment more effective with respect to pain and function than conventional therapy.
Nonoperative management includes bed rest, partial weightbearing with crutches, or weightbearing as tolerated.

Physical therapy (PT) can be useful to restore motion and improve gait. Cochrane authors found no difference between hip core decompression and PT compared with PT alone in a single trial of patients with sickle cell disease and avascular necrosis.
There are insufficient data to support bracing in patients with Legg-Calve-Perthes disease; Petrie casts may play a role in short-term treatment prior to complete reossification.
Electrical stimulation, pulsed electromagnetic fields, and trials of vasoactive medications have not met with success or have not been well studied.
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy may be a safe and effective method to improve motor function and relieve pain in patients with avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Hyperbaric oxygen treatment for pre-collapse avascular necrosis of the femoral head is considered a safe alternative with satisfactory clinical and radiological outcomes and low complications rate.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies with 619 patients (855 hips) found the application of stem cell therapy in early-stage osteonecrosis of the femoral head delayed femoral head collapse (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.33-0.89) and total hip replacement (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34-0.90). There were no significant differences in adverse events between the stem cell and control groups. Study heterogeneity, however, was high.

Compared with core decompression (CD) alone in the treatment of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, combined CD and autologous bone marrow stem cell implantation had better pain relief and clinical outcomes and delayed the collapse of the femoral head more effectively (see surgical therapy section).
Once avascular necrosis is diagnosed, refer to an orthopedic surgeon for staging and consideration of surgical treatment to preserve the femoral head.
Surgical complications may include nonunion, malunion, peroneal nerve palsy, deep vein thrombosis, intraoperative fractures, and postoperative dislocation.
Progression is proportional to lesion size, with small lesions (less than 15% of femoral head involvement) less likely to progress. B
Large lesions (more than 30% of femoral head involvement) are likely to progress to collapse despite treatment. B
The natural history of avascular necrosis is not well understood.

In patients with smaller lesions in non-weightbearing areas, symptoms tend to resolve without femoral head collapse or arthritis. In one systematic review, lesions involving <15% of the femoral head or necrotic angle of less than 200° (14%-25% progress) and lesions involving only the medial 1/3 of the weightbearing surface (about 5% progress) were least likely to progress.
In those with larger lesions and/or sustained vascular insult to the femoral head, collapse and secondary arthritis develop.

In one long-term (mean 20.4 years) follow-up study of 56 patients with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, few patients required surgical intervention (three had hip arthroplasty and one had pelvic osteotomy) but most had mild (N = 16) or moderate to severe (N = 24) osteoarthritic changes on radiographs. On multivariate logistic regression, only the Stulberg classification (type of I or II compared with IV or V) was significantly associated with the Nonarthritic Hip Score (e.g., 60% with type IV had a poor or fair outcome on the Nonarthritic Hip Score).
In stages prior to femoral head collapse, core decompression has a success rate of approximately 70%.

After femoral head collapse, total hip arthroplasty has been shown to have success rates over 90%; however, the failure rate is still three to four times more common with osteonecrosis than with osteoarthritis.
Total hip arthroplasty fails in almost 60% of patients with avascular necrosis due to sickle cell disease.
Consider sickle-cell testing in African-American patients.
Lipid profile.
Screening for coagulopathies (protein C and S deficiencies, factor V Leiden).
Annual plain radiographs if stage 0 or 1A and managing conservatively, to watch for progression.
Advise patients to abstain from alcohol and stop smoking.
Good control of diabetes and lipids may prevent recurrence or progression.
Older, more sedentary patients may benefit most from total hip arthroplasty, even with less severe forms of disease.
Avascular necrosis is rare in pregnancy; similar symptoms may be seen with transient regional osteoporosis.
Two types of avascular necrosis are seen only in children: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease and osteonecrosis associated with slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

Authors of a systematic review of 5 studies of children with leukemia and osteonecrosis found bisphosphonate use combined with supplements and PT compared to supplements and PT alone resulted in less pain (severe in 17% vs. 64%, respectively) and improved mobility (improved/full in 66% vs. 27%, respectively), but no decrease in progressive joint destruction (46% in the bisphosphonate group).

feature.caption: Association of Research Circulation Osseous (ARCO) Staging System for Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Imaging Findings
0 Bone biopsy results consistent with osteonecrosis
Other test results normal
1 Positive findings on bone scan, MRI, or both
Extent of involvement A, B, or Ca
2 Mottled appearance of femoral head, osteosclerosis, cyst formation, and osteopenia on radiographs; no signs of collapse of femoral head on radiographic or CT study
Positive findings on bone scan and MRI; no changes in acetabulum
Extent of involvement A, B, or C
3 Presence of crescent sign lesions classified on basis of appearance on AP and lateral radiographs
Extent of involvement A, B, or C
Further characterization by amount of depression (in millimeters)
4 Articular surface flattened; joint space shows narrowing; changes in acetabulum with evidence of osteosclerosis, cyst formation, and marginal osteophytes
aA, less than 15%; B, 15% to 30%; C, greater than 30% involvement. From ARCO Committee on Terminology and Staging. The ARCO perspective for reaching one uniform staging system for osteonecrosis. Schoutens A, Arlet J, Gardeniers JW, Hughes SP. Bone Circulation and Vascularization in Normal and Pathological Conditions: Proceedings of a NATO ARW Held in Brussels, Belgium, September 25-26, 1992. 1st. New York: Plenum Press. 1993; 375-380.
